relationships.note: Its family is the sister group of poison frogs

name: Trinidadian stream frog
biology: Measures about 2.5–3 cm, brown with dark stripes. Females have a bright yellow throat bordered by a dark collar; males have grey throats that turn black when calling. It eats small insects.
behaviour: Active by day. Females defend territories along streams and display their yellow throats to rivals. Males call from rocks and carry tadpoles on their backs to pools.
conservation: Not considered globally threatened, but limited to one island and vulnerable to changes in stream habitat.
evolution: Mannophryne, the collared frogs, includes about 20 species in Venezuela, Trinidad and Tobago. They are relatives of the poison frogs but do not sequester toxins. Trinidad was joined to South America until about 10,000 years ago.
specialFeatures: It is non-toxic, unlike its poison frog relatives.

name: Leopard tortoise
biology: Measures 40–70 cm and commonly weighs up to about 18 kg, making it one of Africa's largest tortoises. It has a high, domed shell with black blotches. It eats grasses, succulents and thistles. Females lay several clutches of 5–30 eggs, and incubation can take many months. The nest temperature determines the hatchlings' sex. Leopard tortoises can live 80–100 years.
behaviour: Wanders widely in search of food and water. It gnaws bones and eats hyena droppings for calcium. Males ram and try to flip rivals during the breeding season.
conservation: Least Concern.
evolution: A tortoise (Testudinidae), the only species in its genus. Tortoises descend from water-dwelling turtles that moved onto land.
specialFeatures: It gnaws bones and eats hyena droppings to get calcium for its shell. Unlike most tortoises, it can swim.

name: Milk snake
range: North, Central and northern South America
biology: Measures 50–150 cm, with red, black and yellow or white bands. It eats rodents, lizards, birds' eggs and other snakes, and is partly resistant to some snake venoms. Females lay 3–24 eggs in rotting logs or leaf litter.
behaviour: Nocturnal and secretive, spending the day under logs and rocks. It kills prey by constriction. When threatened it vibrates its tail and may release a foul musk.
conservation: Least Concern.
evolution: A kingsnake (Lampropeltis). A 2014 study split the milk snake into seven species. Its bands mimic venomous coral snakes, an example of Batesian mimicry.
specialFeatures: Its red, black and yellow bands mimic those of venomous coral snakes. It is resistant to some snake venom. The name comes from an old myth that it drank milk from cows.

name: Chilean rose tarantula
biology: Leg span is about 12–15 cm. It has eight eyes but poor vision, and senses vibrations through sensitive hairs. Its venom is mild to humans. It liquefies its prey with digestive juices. Females lay about 500 eggs in a silk sac and guard it. It can regrow lost legs when it moults. Females can live over 20 years, while males mature at about five years and die soon after.
behaviour: Nocturnal, living in a burrow and ambushing passing insects. It is docile and can go without food for months. When threatened it flicks irritating hairs from its abdomen.
conservation: Not evaluated by the IUCN; wild collection for the pet trade is a concern.
evolution: A mygalomorph, an ancient branch of spiders whose fangs strike downward. Tarantulas are among the longest-lived terrestrial invertebrates.
specialFeatures: Females can live over 20 years. It flicks irritating hairs from its abdomen at attackers.

name: Macleay's spectre
biology: Females are 15–20 cm long, heavy and spiny, with short wings and cannot fly. Males are thin and can fly. It eats eucalyptus leaves. Females can lay eggs without mating, which hatch into females. The eggs look like seeds and have a knob that attracts ants, which carry them into their nests. Young nymphs mimic ants and run fast with their abdomens curled.
behaviour: Sways like a leaf in the wind to blend in. When threatened it curls its abdomen over its back like a scorpion, raises its spiny legs and releases a smell.
conservation: Not evaluated.
evolution: A stick insect (Phasmatodea). Stick insects are known for elaborate camouflage, and some can lose and later regain wings over evolutionary time.
specialFeatures: Its eggs look like seeds and have a tasty knob that attracts ants. The ants carry the eggs into their nests, where they are protected. Females can lay fertile eggs without mating.

name: Madagascan hissing cockroach
biology: Measures 5–7.5 cm and is wingless. Males have horn-like bumps on the thorax. The female carries her egg case inside her body and gives birth to about 30–60 nymphs. It eats decaying plants and fruit. It lives two to five years.
behaviour: Lives in colonies. Males defend territories and fight by shoving with their horns. It makes three types of hiss by forcing air through its breathing holes: disturbance, courtship and fighting.
conservation: Not evaluated.
evolution: A member of Blaberidae. Termites evolved from within the cockroaches.
specialFeatures: It hisses by pushing air through its breathing holes. Males have horns and fight by shoving.

name: Sun beetle
biology: Measures about 2.5 cm, yellow-green with brown markings. Adults eat fruit and nectar. The larva is a C-shaped grub that eats decaying wood and leaves, and builds a pupal cell from soil.
behaviour: Flies by day and gathers on ripe fruit. It flies with its wing cases closed, sliding its wings out from the sides.
conservation: Not evaluated.
evolution: A flower chafer (Cetoniinae) in the scarab family, related to dung beetles.
specialFeatures: It flies with its wing cases closed, sliding its wings out from the sides.
